chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 451 to 460, Peyanar's mullai decade of the wife who sees the season (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து): the rains have come and her husband, away with the king's army, has not, and she reads frogs, mullai, kondrai, pakanrai, herons and the north wind against her pale shoulders and wasted eyes.

451.reading: The wife asks why the men who left her helpless as the rainy season's morning came should keep back from the feast of welcome their chariot would bring, since holding out in patience, watching over an army no one can turn back, is the king's work and not theirs.
451.nuance: இருத்தல், the mullai word for her own patient waiting, is here handed to the king (ஆற்றவும் இருத்தல் வேந்தனது தொழிலே): she argues that endurance in the camp belongs to his duty, so her husband's share of the war ended when the rains came.

thinai_evidence.note: the morning the rains set in, and a man away with the king's army

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

452.reading: The roaring cloud has spread so the parched earth puts out shoots and has made the rainy season, she says, while her war-loving husband's effort to win tribute has made the pallor bloom like the gold of peerkku flowers on her soft shoulders and hidden their fine beauty.
452.nuance: Two clauses close on the same verb, கார்செய் தன்றே and அலர்செய் தன்றே: the cloud makes the season, his campaign makes her pallor. அலர் is both blossom and the town's talk, so the bloom on her shoulders is also what people will say.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud and the coming of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

453.reading: Frogs crowd every hollow and harsh-voiced flocks of birds cry on every height: look, she says, the rains have begun this morning, and so my long eyes have begun to run with water, and his chariot has begun its way toward us.
453.nuance: Three clauses on தொடங்கு tie the season, her tears and his chariot into one beginning. Whether the tears are of grief or of relief turns on how line 4 is divided, and the poem lets both stand.

thinai_evidence.note: the first morning of the rains

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; உதுக்காண் (look there) is said to someone beside her, taken as the friend

454.reading: As the mullai, clasping the green thalavam creeper and slowly tending its even buds bright as moonlight, reaches out for the rains it longs for, so the beauty of her dark skin stays waiting, longing for his chariot.
454.nuance: The comparison uses the mullai's longing and leaves out one thing it shows: the mullai waits clasped to a partner creeper (தழீஇ), which she does not have.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai flower reaching for the rains

comparisons.tenor: her beauty longing for his chariot

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

455.reading: So that the kings' war may cool, the loud cloud, raging with a war drum's sound, has begun the rains, she says, and pitiable, pitiable indeed are her broad soft shoulders, their glow turned pale, the bright bangles slipping, wasted and stripped of their old beauty.
455.nuance: The rain itself ends the campaign (அரசுபகை தணிய): the season that should free him has come, so the pity she spends on her own shoulders is also a charge that he is late.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains beginning, which halt the kings' war

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

456.reading: She asks her friend whether they have stopped thinking of us, those who assured us we would live here together through the cold season of hard dew and went away, now that the great white-petalled pakanrai flowers, like the moon by day, on white creepers deck the green eengai bushes.
456.nuance: The season named is கூதிர், the cold season, which the Tholkappiyam gives to kurinji; this decade carries the mullai wait past the rains into the dews, so his promise has already overrun its time.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting on a promise to be together through the season

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; she names the friend (தோழி, line 1)

457.reading: In this season hard to be apart in, when flocks of herons cry out, unable to escape the falling dew that torments them, she tells her simple heart that her lover cannot leave her and rest content, and it cannot forget him and rest.
457.nuance: The two halves turn on the same verb, அமைகல்லார் and அமைகல்லாது: neither he nor her heart can settle. The crying herons were not tagged iraicchi: they suffer and cry, which carries a mood, but do nothing a person of the situation does or should do.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the season for a man who will not stay away

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season; the poem closes on என் மடங்கெழு நெஞ்சே, her own heart

458.reading: The kondrai's clustered pods have ripened into long pipe-like fruit, and its cool flowers that met the thundering rain lie wet and scattered: they look like her eyes, which lost their fine beauty when the lord of the bards went away.
458.nuance: The kondrai is the mullai sign that the rains, and so his promised return, have come; here it has already flowered, fruited and been beaten down, so it marks how far past the promise the season has run. The hero is named by பாணர் பெருமகன், a marutham epithet.

thinai_evidence.note: the kondrai of the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes that lost their beauty

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

459.reading: She wonders whether she will be able to embrace, so that the pallor leaves her soft, bamboo-round shoulders, the fragrant cool chest of the man of the town of good fields, who went with the victorious king whose glorious army crossed the forts of his enemies.
459.nuance: The cure for pallor is not his return in general but touch (புல்லவும்); the doubt (இயைவது கொல்லோ) is whether the king's war will allow it. He is called ஊரன், the marutham man, though the decade is mullai.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting for a man gone with the king's army

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

460.reading: The fiercely angry king does not tire of his war camp, no message comes from the lord of the loud hill, and the cruel north wind beats on her too, shaking the plantain with its crowded leaves to its whole trunk: what will become of her, she asks, pitiable as she is.
460.nuance: The plantain shaken to the root by the north wind matches her state, but only as a single match of mood, so it is scene, not ullurai. The hero is a வெற்பன், a hill man, and the plantain is a kurinji plant, set in a mullai wait.

thinai_evidence.note: waiting for word from a man held at the king's camp

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the decade title (பருவங்கண்டு கிழத்தி யுரைத்த பத்து) says the wife speaks on seeing the season

links.note: In Akananuru 214 the man in the rain-soaked camp says the war is ours (அமரும் நம்வயினதுவே) while the king does not sleep; in Ainkurunuru 451 the wife says holding out in camp is the king's work (வேந்தனது தொழிலே), not her husband's.
links.teaches: On the same rainy-season campaign the soldier claims the war as his own duty and the wife assigns it wholly to the king, so the mullai situation is a dispute over where a man's obligation ends, and each side rests on a reading of whose war it is.

links.note: Both open with frogs in every hollow (அவல்தோறு, அவல்தொறும்) and the formula கார்தொடங் கின்றே/கின்றால் காலை; in Akananuru 364 the woman concludes that he in the king's camp does not think of us, in Ainkurunuru 453 that his chariot has set out toward us.
links.teaches: The same signs of the first rains, in nearly the same words, lead one wife to despair and another to expect the chariot, so the season's onset in mullai poetry is not itself a message: its meaning is decided by what the woman believes of the man.

links.note: Kural 1234: with the partner gone, the shoulders lose their old beauty (தொல்கவின்) and the bangles slip; Ainkurunuru 455: the shoulders, their bangles loosened, have lost their old beauty (தொன்னலம்) just as the rains begin that stop the kings' war.
links.teaches: The couplet states the wasting of the shoulders as the general mark of separation; the Ainkurunuru poem times it to the rains that end the campaign, so the slipping bangle becomes evidence that he is overdue, not only that he is away.

links.note: Akananuru 24: in the last days of the cold rains, when the pakanrai opens, the man in the king's camp pictures his wife crossing the cold nights alone; Ainkurunuru 456: in the dewy cold season of pakanrai, the wife asks whether the men who promised to stay do not think of her.
links.teaches: Her question in 456, does he not think of us, is answered in Akananuru 24, where in the same pakanrai season he does think of her from the camp, so the pair shows that remembering runs both ways while neither lover can know it.

links.note: Kural 1231: thinking of him who went far, her eyes are ashamed before fragrant flowers; Ainkurunuru 458: the rain-beaten kondrai flowers have come to resemble her eyes, which lost their beauty when he left.
links.teaches: The couplet's eyes lose a contest with flowers they once outshone; the Ainkurunuru poem reverses the direction, bringing the flowers down to the state of the eyes, so the wasted eyes become the measure the season is read by.

links.note: Kural 1265: once she has seen her husband to her eyes' fill the pallor of her soft shoulders will leave; Ainkurunuru 459: she asks whether she can embrace his chest so the pallor of her shoulders goes, while he is away with the king.
links.teaches: Both name the husband's presence as the cure for pallor, but the couplet makes the cure sight while the Ainkurunuru wife makes it embrace and doubts it is possible at all, because the king's war, not the man, decides when he comes.

links.note: In 451 the wife argues that endurance in the camp is the king's work, not her husband's; in 460 she admits the king does not weary of the camp and no message comes.
links.teaches: Read in order, the decade moves from argument to helplessness: the claim in 451 that the king alone should bear the camp turns in 460 into the recognition that the king's appetite for the camp is exactly what holds her husband there.

source_issues.issue: The colophon has no thurai for any poem of this decade; speakers in thurai_akam are taken from the decade title and the poems.
நெடுங்கணவர் is run together; it divides as நெடுங்கண் அவர் (my long eyes; his chariot), on which the sense of the line turns. Marked uncertain.
உருவைல் is not a regular form; the sense (like the moon by day) wants உருவின். The word is not used as evidence.
மெலிறை looks like a dropped consonant for மெல்லிறை (soft-jointed); the word is not used as evidence.
